summary: Elk County, PA steel Blaw-Knox tower built 1922 and dismantled 1976; a 330-foot state telecom tower occupies the site with a 12-by-16-foot shelter built in 2002, and only concrete piers remain.

facts.status_note: Dismantled in 1976. A 330-foot state telecommunications tower and a 12-by-16-foot shelter built in 2002 occupy the site; the township says only the concrete piers of the old tower can still be located.
facts.agency: Pennsylvania Department of Forests & Waters (built the tower in 1922)

events.note: Constructed by the Pennsylvania Department of Forests & Waters; steel Blaw-Knox tower per the register
12 by 16 foot equipment shelter constructed in 2002 on the site; the source does not date the 330-foot state telecommunications tower

evidence.supports: Steel Blaw-Knox tower built in 1922 and removed in 1976
evidence.quote: This steel Blaw-Knox tower was built in 1922 and removed in 1976.

evidence.supports: 1926 newspaper item: highest point in Elk county, altitude 2,340
evidence.quote: From the Wildwood fire tower on the highest point of Elk county, altitude 2,340, you have a fine view over miles of the refuge and adjoining forest.

evidence.supports: Built by the Pennsylvania Department of Forests & Waters in 1922

evidence.quote: It stood near a ridge along the continental divide just east of the Shawmut Railroad grade in the Straight Creek area of Jones Township.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives 2,375 ft (724 m), matching the brief's 723.9 m. A 1926 newspaper item gives an altitude of 2,340 feet. The story gives both figures and says they disagree.

notes_for_editor: The 1922 build date and 1976 removal agree across the register and the township page. The 2,340 ft figure is from a 1926 newspaper item quoted on the Forest Lookouts page and was not checked against the paper; the quoted text gives no unit, and feet is inferred. Do not mix in a Facebook post about a different 1922 Blaw-Knox tower moved from Sideling Hill to the Pennsylvania Lumber Museum; it is not this tower. The site is now a state telecommunications facility; no source describes public access, so do not suggest visitors enter it. No staffing or fire record was found in the sources read. The second search added nothing new.
